Tangent support and analytic directions

Exposition, proofs and exercises: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

There are two different geometries at a singular point. The support has directions in physical space along which it approaches the point. The analytic wavefront has a closed set of directions in the cotangent fiber. A normal to this latter set must point along the physical tangent cone, with both signs. This relation propagates analytic regularity through convex regions of a fiber and explains why analytic Cauchy data control all normal frequencies near a noncharacteristic boundary. An explicit smooth counterexample shows the force of the analytic hypothesis.

Pairings are complex-linear, , and the Fourier sign is . A Euclidean scalar product identifies vectors and covectors when distances or normals are taken inside one fiber. Analytic changes of coordinates retain the intrinsic tangent and cotangent meanings.

The Gaussian transform of a compact hyperfunction, represented by an analytic functional, is The distance estimate, local representative independence and exact exponential criterion for analytic wavefronts are Gaussian windows and analytic directions, Theorems 1 and 4 and Corollary 5. The finite closed-cone decomposition and its holomorphic sides are Directional splitting and holomorphic compatibility, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2. Analyticity when the whole fiber is regular, and agreement with the distributional analytic wavefront, are Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Theorem 3; its Theorem 7 gives the converse holomorphic wedge representation used in Theorem 2 below. Compact representatives and localization are proved in Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources.

The geometry of supporting functions and their strict quadratic replacements is Both analytic directions at support boundaries, (1)–(4); its Theorem 4 proves the convex contact assertion used below. The maximum principle is Positive derivatives and canonical representatives, Theorem 3.4, and subharmonicity of the logarithm of a holomorphic function is Compactness and complex-line positivity, Proposition 3.2. Finite-dimensional compactness, derivatives, integration and limiting operations use the supplied scalar and integration foundations.
